documents.text:
SwimSight: AI-Assisted Swimming Intelligence Platform

Project documentation: competition monitoring, rule-compliance support, performance analytics, and athlete coaching

Working title: SwimSight (final name to be chosen in Appendix B; trademark and domain availability must be checked). Document status: v1.0 draft, written 8 October 2026. All rule references and market facts must be re-verified before the final submission (see References).

How to read this document. Parts 1 to 4 follow the 45-section structure you specified. Section 0 (below) is the critical review that shaped the design. Every AI technique is described with WHAT / WHY / INPUT / OUTPUT / LIMITATION / EVALUATION. Anything that is an assumption is labelled [ASSUMPTION] . Anything that depends on official rules is labelled [RULE-DEPENDENT] and must be checked against the current World Aquatics text.

Revision v2 (9 October 2026). The project is now a dual-mode platform : SwimCoach AI (training intelligence) and SwimComp AI (competition intelligence) on one shared SwimSight infrastructure, plus a technique-related injury-risk screening module. Part I (Sections 0 to 45 below) remains the shared technical and business baseline. Part II (after Appendix C, starting at "Part II") is the v2 master document in the new 32-section structure, and it overrides Part I where they differ: the chatbot in Part I Section 25 is the SwimCoach AI (training) assistant, and the competition product has no chatbot of its own. It also adds the technology stack and detailed hardware tiers that Part I lacked.

0. Critical Review of the Idea (done before writing the design)

0.1 What is strong

- The problem is real: a coach or official cannot continuously observe 8 to 10 swimmers across stroke mechanics, lanes, turns, and rules.

- The pipeline (detect, track, identify, measure, explain) maps cleanly to well-studied CV problems, so each module can be evaluated separately.
- The combination of measured analytics, evidence-backed warnings, and a grounded chatbot is a defensible integration contribution.

0.2 What is weak or over-ambitious in the original brief

  Issue                                                           Why it is a problem                                                                                                                                                                        Practical fix                                                                                                                                                                                                       

  "Detect rule violations" as one feature                         Rules differ per stroke and several cannot be judged reliably from visible cameras (for example, a single downward butterfly kick count, or whether a hand touched the wall underwater).   Split into three tiers: measurable (lane position, 15 m mark, wall contact candidates), assistive (stroke-phase flags for referee review), out of scope (anything needing underwater close-ups or human judgment).  
  Facial recognition for identity                                 Caps, goggles, splash, rear views, underwater. Also high privacy risk.                                                                                                                     Identity comes from registration (heat sheet + lane) plus tracking continuity. Appearance embeddings are a recovery aid, faces optional and off by default.                                                         
  Real-time everything                                            Pose + ReID + multi-camera on one GPU is heavy.                                                                                                                                            Real-time only for tracking, lane state, and position. Pose, technique, and reports run near-real-time or post- race.                                                                                               
  Absolute metrics (m/s, stroke length) from uncalibrated video   Perspective, refraction, and camera shake corrupt them.                                                                                                                                    Calibrate each camera to the pool plane using known pool geometry (lane lines, floats, wall marks). Report error bars.                                                                                              

  Issue                                Why it is a problem                                     Practical fix                                                                                                                          

  Chatbot that "coaches"               An LLM can hallucinate numbers or give unsafe advice.   LLM never computes; it narrates numbers fetched from the database by tools, with a fact-checking layer.                                
  Claiming novelty from "using YOLO"   Not a contribution.                                     Contribution is the integration : lane-aware identity, evidence-grounded warnings, and measured- data-grounded coaching (Section 38).  

0.3 Difficulty and feasibility map

  Component                           Difficulty     Undergrad- feasible?              Needs underwater camera?     Main false- positive risk          

  Swimmer detection (overhead/side)   Medium         Yes                               No                           Splash, reflections, lane floats   
  Tracking with lane prior            Medium         Yes                               No                           ID switches at turns and crowding  
  Cross-camera ReID                   High           Partially (2 cameras, one heat)   No                           Identical caps and suits           
  Lane compliance                     Medium         Yes                               No                           Perspective error, waves           
  Stroke counting (surface strokes)   Medium         Yes                               No                           Double counting, occlusion         
  Pose estimation above water         Medium- High   Yes (pretrained + fine-tune)      No                           Water occlusion                    

  Component                         Difficulty     Undergrad- feasible?         Needs underwater camera?     Main false- positive risk      

  Underwater pose / kick analysis   High           Advanced only                Yes                          Refraction, bubbles            
  Distance/velocity                 Medium         Yes with calibration         No                           Homography drift               
  Turn/wall events                  Medium- High   Yes (candidate events)       Helpful                      Occlusion at wall              
  Rule candidates                   High           Only 2 to 4 selected rules   Some                         Under-observed events          
  Fatigue indicators                Medium         Yes, trend statistics        No                           Confounded by pacing strategy  
  Grounded chatbot                  Medium         Yes                          No                           Hallucination, tone            

0.4 Rules that this system cannot reliably judge from typical views (human-in-theloop only)

- Anything requiring simultaneity or exact positions of limbs underwater (for example, hands and feet touching the wall, kick counts in the first underwater phase) unless underwater cameras and strong evidence review exist.
- Start reaction (false start) and official touch times. These are handled by the startingblock and touchpad systems used at official events. This project must not replace them.
- Any decision to disqualify. The system only produces candidates with evidence .

0.5 Practical compromises adopted

1. Official timing stays with official equipment; SwimSight uses video-derived timing only for analytics, with measured error.
2. The graduation MVP targets one stroke (freestyle) fully , a second (backstroke or breaststroke) partially, and 2 to 4 rule-candidate detectors.
3. All warnings are labelled potential or suspected and always open a review package.
4. Positioning: AI-assisted swimming intelligence , not AI refereeing.

1. Executive Summary

Swimming organizations record a lot of video but extract little structured intelligence from it. SwimSight is a multi-camera computer-vision platform that turns pool video into continuous, measurable, explainable athlete intelligence. It detects and tracks each swimmer, keeps a stable Swimmer ID separate from the tracker's Track ID and from the swimmer's assigned and current lane , measures distance, velocity, strokes, turns, and technique from calibrated pool coordinates, and flags potential rule or lane issues with timestamped video evidence for human officials. After each race it produces a personalized report and feeds a coaching chatbot (working name SwimCoach AI ) that answers athlete questions from the athlete's own measured history in a supportive, motivating tone.

Key design principles

- Identity from registration + continuity, not faces.
- Deterministic rules, never an LLM, decide whether a rule condition was met.
- Every warning carries evidence, confidence, and a rule reference with version.
- The chatbot narrates data; it does not invent data.
- Human officials and coaches always keep the final decision.

Realistic outcome for an undergraduate team: a working system on recorded training and mock-competition video from a real pool with 2 to 3 cameras, demonstrating tracking, lane compliance, stroke counting, calibrated speed and distance, turn analytics, a small set of rule candidates with evidence, reports, and a grounded chatbot, all evaluated with quantitative metrics.

2. Introduction

Competitive swimming is decided by hundredths of a second, and small technique differences (stroke length, turn quality, underwater phase) explain much of the result. Official timing is already highly automated (touchpads, start systems). Technique, pacing, and compliance analysis are still largely manual. Recent research and startups show that vision-based swimming analytics is now feasible; for example, a WACV 2026 paper reports overhead drone footage used to classify strokes, estimate speed, lap time, and stroke count, and Omega has stated it uses computer vision to track swimmers'

acceleration, deceleration, stroke count and time in the water at the Paris 2024 Olympics. This project builds an integrated, explainable, athlete-centred platform rather than a single-purpose model.

3. Problem Statement

Swimming organizations have large amounts of video data but limited automated intelligence extracted from that data.

Concretely, coaches and officials cannot continuously and consistently track, for every swimmer at once: identity and lane, technique, stroke cycles, distance and speed, turns and underwater phase, possible rule issues, and degradation during a race. Post-race analysis is slow, manual, and inconsistent; feedback to every athlete is rarely personalized.

Technical problem statement. Given synchronized multi-camera video of a multi-lane pool and a pre-registered heat sheet, estimate for each swimmer a stable identity, a calibrated trajectory in pool coordinates, stroke-cycle and technique descriptors, and rule-relevant events, with confidence and evidence, and convert those measurements into personalized, grounded feedback.

4. Business Problem

  Coaches                  Cannot watch all swimmers; delayed feedback   Live lane view, post-set summaries, degradation alerts   Higher coaching quality at scale      Minutes from race end to feedback                 
  Professional athletes    Need granular biomechanics and trend data     Calibrated metrics, stroke- length and turn trends       Marginal gains                        Metric repeatability vs manual annotation         
  Federations              Inconsistent analytics across clubs           Standardized, auditable metrics                          Talent identification, benchmarking   Coverage of events analyzed                       
  Competition organizers   Few staff to review events                    Evidence packages shorten review                         Lower officiating load                Review time per flagged event                     
  Referees / officials     Must watch many lanes; disputes               Candidate events with clips and measurements             Faster, more consistent review        Candidate precision / recall                      
  Performance centers      Manual notation of races                      Automated race analysis                                  Throughput                            Races analyzed per analyst-day

Business problems investigated: expensive manual analysis, limited coach attention, inability to analyze every swimmer continuously, delayed feedback, inconsistent manual measurement, review of suspicious events, limited historical intelligence, lack of personalized feedback, lack of scalable analytics, and difficulty spotting technical deterioration.

5. Proposed Solution

SwimSight converts video to intelligence in five stages: Sense (cameras and calibration), Identify (detect, track, ReID, lane binding), Measure (pose, strokes, distance, velocity, turns), Reason (lane state machine, rule engine, evidence), Communicate (dashboards, reports, SwimCoach AI).

```
Cameras -> Ingest -> Detect -> Track -> ReID/Lane binding -> Fusion -> Pose -> Temporal models -> Stroke/Turn/Technique -> Distance/Velocity -> Lane state machine -> Rule engine -> Evidence -> Analytics -> DB -> Reports -> Chatbot -> Dashboards
```

Positioning: AI-assisted swimming intelligence. The AI measures, flags, explains, and coaches; humans decide.

6. Project Objectives

1. Detect and track all swimmers in a pool with a stable Swimmer ID (target IDF1 and IDswitch numbers set in Section 31).
2. Bind each swimmer to the registered assigned lane and compute current lane continuously.
3. Detect persistent lane deviation using a temporal state machine.
4. Estimate calibrated distance, velocity, acceleration, and lap splits.
5. Count strokes and compute stroke rate, stroke length, and consistency.
6. Recognize stroke style and score technique from pose sequences.
7. Detect turns, wall events, underwater phase, and finish candidates.
8. Raise evidence-backed, human-reviewed potential-violation candidates for a small, verified rule set .
9. Produce per-swimmer reports and fatigue-related trend indicators.
10. Provide a grounded, motivational chatbot using the swimmer's own data.
11. Deliver dashboards for coach, referee-review, and athlete.

7. Target Users

Data flow in one line: frames, boxes, tracks, identities, pool coordinates, poses, events, rule candidates, evidence, analytics, reports, chat answers.

11. Camera and Hardware Architecture

11.1 Camera roles

  Camera                             Placement                                    Purpose                                                          Notes                                                                                                  

  Overhead / elevated wide           Above the pool or on a high gantry/ceiling   Lane geometry, global trajectories, lane compliance, positions   Best for homography; perspective is simplest. Reflections still occur.                                 
  Side-view (pool deck, long axis)   Along the pool, tracking pan or fixed wide   Stroke mechanics, body line, breathing                           Perspective changes strongly with distance. Use multiple fixed cameras to avoid pan- tilt complexity.  
  End-of-pool                        Behind start/turn ends                       Turn approach, wall contact candidate, head-surface events       Occlusion by lane ropes/blocks.                                                                        
  Underwater                         Pool wall windows or mounted housings        Underwater kicks, breakout, wall touch evidence                  Required for any reliable underwater analysis; highest cost and installation effort.                   
  High-frame-rate                    Selected angles                              Fast events (entry, turn rotation)                               Use only where needed; storage heavy.                                                                  

11.2 Multi-camera fusion

WHAT: combine detections from several cameras into one coherent swimmer trajectory in pool coordinates. WHY: one camera is occluded or has poor resolution at far lanes; multiple views improve robustness. INPUT: per-camera tracks with timestamps, camera calibrations, lane geometry, registration data. OUTPUT: fused trajectory (x along pool, y across, time) per Swimmer ID. LIMITATION: clock drift, calibration error, similar-looking swimmers, missing overlap between views. EVALUATION: cross-camera association accuracy, IDF1 on fused tracks, position error vs. ground truth.

Synchronization. Hardware sync (PTP or a genlock-capable setup) is preferred; the lowbudget approach is a visible sync event (start LED or a clap or horn recorded on audio) plus NTP and per-clip offset estimation by cross-correlating motion or audio.

Calibration and coordinates.

- Define the pool coordinate frame: origin at the start wall and lane 1 edge, x along the length, y across lanes, z above water. Lane width and pool length come from the facility specification (to be measured on site; do not assume).
- Estimate a homography H from image pixels to the water-plane (x, y) using at least 4 known points (lane-line intersections, floats marks, 5 m flags, wall corners). Refine with RANSAC and many points.
- Intrinsic calibration (checkerboard) removes lens distortion before homography.
- Swimmers are 3D objects partly submerged; use the waterline point (for example, the head/shoulder at the surface) rather than the box center to map to the plane. Refraction affects underwater cameras and requires separate calibration.

Cross-camera association example.

```
Camera A Track 17  (overhead)  -> pool (x=12.4 m, y=3.1 m) at t=12.34 s Camera B Track 42  (side)      -> pool (x=12.5 m, y=3.0 m) at t=12.34 s Same lane prior = 4, speed continuity OK, appearance similarity 0.81 => association score 0.93 -> both belong to Swimmer ID 1933
```

Association uses a cost combining spatial distance in pool coordinates, lane agreement, velocity direction, time offset, and appearance similarity, solved with Hungarian matching and gated by thresholds.

Pool environments add humidity, chlorine, glare, and reflections: use appropriate enclosures, polarizing filters, and fixed exposure settings. Safety and installation approval from the facility is mandatory.

12. Swimmer Identification and Re-Identification

12.1 Four separate concepts

  Concept         Meaning                                         Lifetime                 Who assigns it       

  Swimmer ID      Permanent identity (e.g., 1933)                 Across events            Registration system  
  Track ID        Temporary tracker label per camera (e.g., 17)   Until the track breaks   Tracker              
  Assigned Lane   Lane from the heat sheet (e.g., 4)              One heat                 Competition data     
  Current Lane    Lane geometrically occupied now                 Per frame                Geometry             

Why they must be separate. A tracker's Track ID changes after occlusion, splash, or a turn, so it cannot be an identity. A swimmer's assigned lane is policy, while the current lane is an observation; if they were one field, a lane deviation could never be detected, and a lane-tied identity could be wrongly reassigned to another swimmer. Keeping four fields lets the system say: "Track 17 is currently believed to be Swimmer 1933 (confidence 0.96), assigned to Lane 4, currently in Lane 4."

```
{ "swimmer_id": 1933, "camera_id": "cam_overhead_1", "track_id": 17, "assigned_lane": 4, "current_lane": 4, "identity_confidence": 0.96, "binding_source": ["lane_prior", "trajectory", "appearance"] }
```

12.2 Registration stage

Fields: swimmer ID, name, team, competition, heat, assigned lane, reference images (cap/suit colors, front/back), appearance descriptor, optional identity embedding. Registration happens before the race from the heat sheet. For minors or privacy-sensitive settings, store pseudonymous IDs and no face embeddings.

12.3 Identity strategy (priority order)

1. Lane prior (strongest in competition): at the start, each lane contains exactly one registered swimmer. Initial binding is assigned by lane geometry.
2. Temporal continuity: Kalman-filter motion and association (ByteTrack/BoT-SORT) maintain Track ID.
3. Trajectory and order: swimmers in adjacent lanes rarely swap; position order and speed constrain identity.
4. Appearance embedding: body/cap/suit features from a ReID network for recovery after occlusion.
5. Camera transition timing: expected time of arrival in the next camera from speed and distance.
6. Optional face: only when visible and consented; never required.

Identity score is a weighted combination (weights tuned on validation data, not guessed):

S = w1lane + w2motion + w3appearance + w4camera\_timing (+ w5face) . Bind when S exceeds a threshold with a margin over the second-best candidate; otherwise mark the identity uncertain and propagate uncertainty to downstream metrics instead of guessing.

12.4 Recovery after occlusion or tracking failure

- Keep a lost track buffer with the last pool position and velocity.
- Predict where the swimmer should reappear (constant-velocity model in pool coordinates, constrained to the lane).
- On a new track in the predicted region, compute embedding similarity and lane agreement; re-bind if the margin is sufficient.
- If two swimmers cross lanes or both vanish, defer binding and use later evidence (for example, finish order or the next wall) with retroactive correction logged in an audit trail.

WHAT (ReID): learns an embedding where the same swimmer has similar vectors across views. WHY: to re-link tracks after occlusion. INPUT: person crops (above water). OUTPUT: a 128 to 512-d embedding. LIMITATION: identical caps/suits (team uniforms) make appearance weak; underwater views look different; use lane/motion as primary. EVALUATION: Rank-1, mAP, CMC, and in-pipeline IDF1 and ID switches, with identitydisjoint splits (Section 28).

13. Multi-Object Tracking

WHAT: assigns a consistent Track ID to each detected swimmer across frames. WHY: all later metrics need a continuous trajectory. INPUT: detections (box, confidence, optional keypoints). OUTPUT: tracks (ID, box, pool-plane position, velocity). LIMITATION: swimmers are small, partially submerged, similar in appearance, and heavily occluded by splash and lane ropes. EVALUATION: MOTA, IDF1, HOTA, ID switches, fragmentation.

Detector. A YOLO-family detector (via Ultralytics) fine-tuned on pool data with classes swimmer\_surface , swimmer\_underwater , head , lane\_rope\_float , wall\_marker . Rationale: fast, easy to fine-tune, good tooling. Check the current licence terms of the library you pick (some YOLO releases use AGPL, which matters for commercial deployment); alternatives such as RT-DETR or MMDetection models can be compared.

Tracker. ByteTrack (uses low-confidence detections to keep tracks through splash) and BoT-SORT (adds camera-motion compensation and optional ReID) are the two baselines to compare. Pool-specific upgrades that are the real engineering value:

- Lane-constrained motion model: the Kalman state lives in pool coordinates; lateral motion is bounded by lane width, so tracks cannot jump lanes without strong evidence.

- Lane-gated association: a detection can only be matched to tracks whose predicted lane is the same or adjacent.
- Direction-aware prediction at walls: at the turn, expected velocity reverses; the model switches mode when a wall event is expected.

Failure handling. Track fragmentation is expected near walls and during splash. Fragments are merged by the identity layer (Section 12.4), never by the tracker alone.

14. Lane Compliance

WHAT: determines whether each swimmer remains in the assigned lane and raises a potential lane-deviation candidate if the deviation is meaningful and persistent. WHY: manual monitoring of every lane is inconsistent. INPUT: fused pool-plane trajectory, lane geometry, assigned lane. OUTPUT: per-frame lane state plus events. LIMITATION: homography error, waterline ambiguity, waves, occlusion. EVALUATION: event-level precision/recall, false-positive rate per hour, detection latency.

Continuously computed quantities per swimmer: assigned lane, current lane (argmax of lane intervals containing the waterline point), signed distance from the lane centerline d\_c(t) , distance to nearest lane boundary d\_b(t) , lateral velocity, deviation duration, and a position uncertainty from calibration residuals.

Natural movement vs. meaningful deviation. A swimmer naturally drifts within the lane; arms extend beyond the body midline; breathing shifts the head. Meaningful deviation means the swimmer's reference point (body center projected to the plane) is outside the assigned lane interval by more than the position uncertainty for a sustained period. The thresholds (margin, duration) are configurable parameters tuned on validation data and checked against what officials consider reportable; no value is hard-coded from the rules here.

State machine:

```
 d_c  > T1 for >= N1 frames NORMAL ------------------------------> SUSPICIOUS ^   = N2 ----                                                outside lane interval (by margin m)                                           for >= D seconds, consistent in >=2 cues                                         v                              PERSISTENT DEVIATION                                                                                     evidence package built, confidence >= C +-- - verify] What the system measured: Head first detected above the surface at x = ___ m; expected zone limit configured as ___ m (from rule registry). Confidence: 0.91 (detection 0.95, calibration 0.97, view quality 0.88) Evidence: 12 s clip, 3 key frames, trajectory plot Status: Pending human review.  The system does not make official decisions.
```

The blanks are filled from the rule registry and measurements, never from the LLM's memory.

Confidence is a product of calibrated factors (detection confidence, calibration quality, view visibility, temporal consistency). It must be calibrated (reliability diagrams) so "0.9" actually means about 90% precision on validation data.

22. Performance Analytics

Per-swimmer metrics: race time (official when available), distance, average and peak velocity, split times, stroke count, stroke rate, stroke length, turn time, underwater distance, technique score, technique consistency, lane compliance rate, warnings, acceleration/deceleration profile.

Core relations (consistent units; define SR as cycles per second):

- Average velocity v = D / T
- Stroke rate SR = N\_strokes / T (or cycles/min)
- Stroke length SL = D / N\_strokes
- v = SR x SL (approximate; excludes the underwater/turn portions unless computed per free-swimming segment). Compute free-swimming velocity on segments between breakout and the next wall approach.

Interpretation for coaches:

  Pattern                             Possible reading (an interpretation, not a fact)                                                      

  High SR, low SL                     Possibly a "spinning" stroke: fast turnover but poor propulsion per stroke; check catch/pull quality  
  Lower SR, higher SL                 Efficient long stroke; may be strong in distance events but may limit sprint power                    
  SR up, SL down late in race         Compensation for fatigue-related loss of efficiency                                                   
  Faster turns, same stroke metrics   Gains from turn/underwater work rather than free- swimming                                            

Comparison between swimmers is normalized (height/age group/event distance) and shown with caution; athlete-facing comparisons default to self vs. self (Section 25).

23. Fatigue / Performance-Degradation Analysis

WHAT: compares early-race and late-race behavior and flags a possible fatigue-related performance pattern . WHY: helps coaches target pacing and endurance work. INPUT: perlap series of SL, SR, speed, symmetry, body angle, cycle-time variability, turn time. OUTPUT: trend slopes, change percentages, a degradation indicator with uncertainty. LIMITATION: pacing strategy, event distance, and turns confound the trends; this is not a medical or physiological diagnosis. EVALUATION: agreement with coach annotations, correlation with split-time decline, stability across repeated efforts.

Indicators (per lap or per 25 m segment): falling SL, rising SR, falling velocity, increasing asymmetry, changing body angle, rising cycle variability, longer cycle time, slower turns.

Method. Fit a robust linear (or piecewise) trend per metric across segments; compare last-third vs. first-third means with confidence intervals (bootstrap); compute a composite Degradation Index DI = sum\_k w\_k  z\_k where z\_k is the standardized change of indicator k and weights are set by coach-validated priorities. Only report DI when at least m indicators agree and data quality is sufficient. Use terms: performance degradation , fatigue-related performance indicators , possible fatigue pattern .

25.4 Safety, fairness, and boundaries

- No medical advice, no diagnosis, no extreme training or weight advice. For pain, injury, dizziness, or health concerns the bot redirects to the coach/medical professional.
- Minors: age-appropriate tone, no body-comparison content, guardian/coach visibility per the club policy.
- Comparisons with other swimmers are limited: default is self-comparison; peer comparisons use anonymized, aggregated benchmarks or only metrics that the other athlete has consented to share. (Technical recommendation, not a legal claim.)
- Uncertainty: if a metric has low confidence (for example, underwater distance without an underwater view), the bot says so.
- Rule warnings: the bot reports status faithfully ("under review", "dismissed", "confirmed by referee") and never tells an athlete they were "disqualified".
- Coach override: coaches can add notes and approve plan suggestions; the bot attributes coach advice to the coach.

WHAT: retrieval-augmented generation lets the chatbot cite approved text (technique guides, rules, team policies) alongside structured data. WHY: to ground explanations in vetted content instead of model memory. INPUT: a query and the athlete context.

OUTPUT: retrieved passages with source ids. LIMITATION: poor chunking, stale rules, irrelevant retrieval. EVALUATION: retrieval recall@k, answer faithfulness, citation correctness, human audit.

Retrieval strategy: hybrid (BM25 + dense), metadata filters (athlete age group, stroke, role), reranking, and a hard cap on retrieved tokens. 28.1 Public data and prior work (to verify before use; licences and availability change)

- Consecutive frames are near-duplicates; deduplicate and group by clip.

30. Training Strategy

1. Detection: start from pretrained weights; fine-tune with heavy augmentation (glare, blur, color jitter, mosaic, scale); hard-negative mining on splash and reflections; evaluate by camera and by lane (far lanes are hardest).
2. Tracking: tune association parameters (not trained) on validation; add lane gating; compare trackers by IDF1/ID switches.
3. ReID: pre-train on public ReID, then fine-tune with triplet loss on pool crops (identitydisjoint split); include cap/suit variation; evaluate Rank-1/mAP .
4. Pose: fine-tune on pool keypoints with visibility heads; use temporal smoothing; evaluate OKS/PCK per joint.
5. Temporal TCN: train on windows of normalized keypoints with class balancing; augment with time-warping, mirroring (swap left/right labels carefully), noise; early stopping on validation F1.
6. Calibration quality: collect more calibration points; fit confidence calibration (temperature scaling/isotonic) for all warning scores.
7. MLOps: DVC/MLflow for data and experiments; model cards; fixed random seeds; versioned train/val/test manifests.
8. Ablations: no-lane-prior, no-ReID, single-camera vs. two-camera, pose vs. no-pose cycle counting.

Approach A: Biomechanical screening (graduation MVP)

WHAT: compares each swimmer's movement features with their own recent baseline and flags persistent, meaningful change. WHY: it is explainable, needs no injury labels, and matches the current evidence. INPUT: per-cycle keypoint features + exposure log. OUTPUT: an observation with supporting cycles and clip, never a forecast. LIMITATION: pose error in water, baseline contamination, no proven link to injury. EVALUATION: agreement with expert (coach/physio) labels, alert frequency, coach usefulness.

- Pattern detectors (each is a configurable, documented feature, not a medical rule): late-session rise in L/R asymmetry; rising cycle-to-cycle variability of entry or recovery path; drift of body rotation or body line from the athlete's baseline; (breaststroke, side view) variability of hip/knee motion across kicks; change in stroke rate/length compensation late in a set.
- Detection logic: robust z-score or percent change vs. the athlete's baseline from the previous N comparable sessions; require persistence over multiple cycles and a minimum pose-confidence; escalate only when it recurs across reps or sessions. Thresholds are tuned parameters validated against expert labels, not copied from literature.
- Exposure context: show distance, reps, week-over-week volume change as context. Do not present a single workload ratio as a risk score; the usefulness of such ratios is debated in sports science [VERIFY before using any index] .
- Status workflow: OBSERVED -> COACH REVIEWED -> (optional) REFERRED TO PROFESSIONAL -> CLOSED. Always "requires human assessment".

CORE

II.30 Future Research and Commercial Expansion

II.31 Conclusion

SwimSight is credible as one platform with two modes because identity, calibration, tracking, pose, strokes, distance, database, and governance are shared, while decision authority, permissions, and latency differ.
